rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Local autonomous inference machines for quantum error correcting codes Abstract: Quantum error correction is the central ingredient in making large-scale quantum computers work. Over the last three decades, we have found increasingly powerful ways of redundantly encoding quantum information so that it can survive physical errors. Yet, a central challenge remains decoding: the task of inferring which errors have occurred from syndrome measurements, and determining how they should be corrected. As quantum processors grow in size, this quantum-classical feedback loop must remain fast and scalable. In this talk, I will discuss an approach to decoding based on a local and distributed framework of measurement, computation and feedback. This perspective naturally gives rise to a family of decoding algorithms built entirely from local information processing and communication. Such decoders are designed to be scalable, while realizing error-correction as a nonequilibrium phase of noise-robust matter. Bio : Sid is a Ph.D. student at Princeton University working at the intersection of many-body physics, quantum information, and algorithms. His research develops mathematical and computational tools for understanding complex quantum systems. Lunch will be provided at 12:00 PM in EQuad J401.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: An Astonishing Quantum Universe in Two Dimensions: From Fundamental Physics to (Possibly) Quantum Computation Abstract: When electrons are confined to two dimensions and subjected to a magnetic field, they enter an astonishing quantum world that defies our everyday intuition. Here, electrons capture quanta of magnetic field and transform into exotic particles known as composite fermions, which reveal a remarkably rich landscape of strongly-correlated quantum states and phenomena, including the fractional quantum Hall effects, strange metals, paired states and crystals. This quantum universe is also thought to harbor emergent particles with non-Abelian statistics, which have inspired proposals for fault tolerant topological quantum computation. I will recount the discoveries and surprises that led to this physics, touch upon the latest developments and discuss how curiosity-driven research into fundamental quantum states may help shape future quantum technologies. The talk is intended for a broad audience and requires no specialized knowledge of condensed-matter physics. A light lunch will be served in the Bowen Atrium at 11:45am. Sponsor Mansour Shayegan

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: When Crystals Flow: The Emergence of Supersolid Quantum States Abstract: The exploration of superfluidity has fascinated scientists for decades, spanning a wide range of systems—from solids and liquids to gases, and even light. Traditionally, the study of superfluid order has been confined to spatially homogeneous systems, where uniform conditions provide a simpler framework for understanding this extraordinary quantum state. But what happens when superfluidity arises in systems with periodic density modulations? Can the inherent localization of periodic structures coexist with the fluid-like properties of a superfluid? Could a solid, with its rigid crystalline structure, exhibit superfluid behavior? Or conversely, might a superfluid reveal a crystalline order? These questions, long at the frontier of quantum many-body physics, naturally extend early theoretical vision into regimes where broken symmetries intertwine. Recent breakthroughs have provided compelling answers with the discovery of “supersolid” quantum states—phases that uniquely combine superfluid and crystalline properties. This talk will delve into the experimental realization of supersolidity in dipolar quantum gases from the point of view of Innsbruck results. Key topics include the dynamics of symmetry breaking, the emergence of phase-coherent density-modulated states, and the observation of quantized vortices in rotating supersolid phases. A light lunch will be served in the Bowen Atrium at 11:45am. Sponsors Sarang Gopalakrishnan Waseem Bakr

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Quantum signatures in molecular polaritonics and other emerging photonic platforms. Abstract: Molecular polaritons emerge when ensembles of molecules strongly couple to confined electromagnetic modes, enabling repeated energy exchange between light and matter. Such interactions are expected to activate nonlinear optical processes, yet many experimental observations remain accurately described by classical optics. We address this paradox from a spectroscopic perspective. We derive a general expression for the polaritonic linear response, showing that widely used classical-optics-based descriptions include a hierarchy of finite-size quantum corrections that encode signatures of nonlinear optical processes, such as Raman scattering mediated by cavity vacuum fluctuations in the linear response. An emergent timescale separation in polaritonic dynamics explains the absence of spectroscopic fingerprints of these nonlinearities in commonly used low-Q cavities; they are expected to emerge in high-Q, discrete-mode cavities like microresonators, where enhanced spectral resolution allows these rare events to manifest. Understanding these nonlinear effects is crucial for harnessing genuine cavity-induced quantum processes for new-generation quantum technologies. References [1] A. Koner✝, J. title: Many body quantum games
speaker: Rahul Nandkishore, University of Colorado, Boulder
content: Title: Many body quantum games Abstract: I will discuss co-ordinational games played on quantum devices from the perspective of many body physics. In the first half of the talk, I will discuss how concepts from many body physics may be used to secure robust and provable quantum advantage at concrete scalable tasks on already existing quantum devices. title: Princeton Quantum Technology Conference 2026
content: The Princeton Quantum Technology Conference (PQTC) aims to bring together visionary speakers from disparate fields that are pushing the frontiers of quantum technology by seriously tackling challenges in quantum hardware and materials, system architecture and scaling, and error correction. The event structure will be designed to allow ample time for discussion and interaction, with the hope of catalyzing new ideas and collaborations.This event is supported by the Princeton Quantum Initiative.Event details
